headline: The audit purge anchor is signed — three statements could erase an audit trail and leave the chain verifying clean
summary:
The purge anchor is the one thing in the audit chain that says rows are ALLOWED to be missing. Every other tamper check compares a stored hash against a recomputed one, so deleting rows leaves a gap that verification catches; the anchor closes that gap by declaration. It was accepted on shape alone — 128 hex characters and a whole number — which is exactly what an attacker with write access supplies. Delete the rows, delete the checkpoints covering them, insert an anchor naming any hash and counter, and `b.audit.verify` reported a clean chain. That is fewer steps than the relink-and-forge attack the chain already refuses, and it erases more.

The anchor now carries a post-quantum signature over every field a reader acts on, and every place that reads it verifies it first: the chain walk, the contiguity guard on the next purge, the predecessor lookup that grounds the next archive's proof, and the append path itself, which needs the boundary to know where a purged chain resumes.

Upgrading with an existing purge anchor requires one boot with `acceptUnsignedPurgeAnchor: true`; see Migration.

items.title: A purge anchor must prove it was written with the audit-signing key (#674)
items.body:
`b.auditChain.verifyChain` adopted `lastPurgedRowHash` as the chain origin and skipped every row at or below `lastPurgedCounter` after checking only that the hash was 128 hex characters and the counter was a whole number. Both are trivially satisfiable by anyone who can write to the database, and the result was a verification that reported success over an arbitrary quantity of deleted history.

The anchor now carries `signature` and `publicKeyFingerprint`, signed by `b.auditSign` over the scope, boundary counter, boundary row hash, archive identifier and purge time. The signed layout is newline-delimited and refuses a newline inside any string field at both sign and verify time, so one signature can never verify two different readings of the same bytes. A boundary counter beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is refused for the same reason: the column is a BIGINT and the signed bytes carry the counter as text, so above that range two distinct stored values render identically and one signature would cover both. The same bound now applies wherever a counter is rendered into bytes that get signed — the consumer chain anchors in `b.auditSign` and the origin a `b.chainWriter` resumes from — through one shared predicate rather than three spellings of it. Its format string is distinct from the checkpoint and consumer-anchor formats, so a signature minted for one can never be replayed as another.

`b.auditChain.verifyPurgeAnchor` reports a status rather than a boolean, because the ways an anchor can fail to verify call for different reactions: `unsigned`, `forged`, `corrupt`, and `unchecked` — the last meaning the process holds no signing key and could not perform the check at all. Collapsing `unchecked` into `forged` would raise a tamper alarm on a healthy volume every time an offline verifier ran, and collapsing it into success would accept anything.

A clean result over a purge now says what was established and what was not: the boundary counter, whether the signature verified, the archive the anchor names, and whether anything actually found it. A signature proves this framework wrote the boundary; it says nothing about whether the archive still exists or holds those rows, and a report that ran the two together would be the wrong thing to hand an auditor.

Only the consumer knows where bundles are kept, so the check is theirs to supply: `b.auditChain.verifyChain(..., { resolveArchive })`, `b.db.init({ resolvePurgeArchive })` for the boot verify, and `blamejs audit verify-chain --archive-dir` for an offline one. With it, a boundary whose archive cannot be produced fails the verify instead of licensing the gap. Both resolvers are refused at the point they are supplied when they are present but not callable: they are consulted only when callable, so a typo or a config that failed to load would remove the very check that was asked for and return a clean result — a gap nothing can ever show the contents of. Without it the walk proceeds and the result says the archive was not resolved.

items.title: The next purge verifies the anchor it is about to extend
items.body:
Checking the anchor only at read time would have left it forgeable through the writer. An unsigned anchor carrying the real predecessor hash, followed by a legitimate purge of the next archive, would have had that purge sign the enlarged boundary — laundering the earlier deletion permanently, under a valid signature.

`b.auditTools.purge` verifies the existing anchor before extending it, and `b.auditTools.exportSlice` verifies it before using its hash to ground the next archive's chain proof. The signature is also computed before the rows are deleted rather than after: signing afterwards means an unavailable key leaves the rows already gone and an unsigned anchor over an unrecoverable deletion, which is the state a reader is now required to refuse. Failing before the delete costs nothing — the archive is on disk and the purge can be re-run.

items.title: A purge is a single-writer operation, start to finish
items.body:
Reading the anchor, deciding the new boundary is contiguous with it, and writing that boundary are one decision. Split across two steps they were two, and two overlapping purges could each find themselves contiguous with the same anchor and each overwrite the other's boundary — leaving rows deleted with nothing accounting for them, which verification then reports as clean, because the anchor is what licenses absence.

The whole sequence now runs under the audit chain's append lock, so an append cannot land between the deletion and the anchor that explains it either. `b.auditTools.purge` and `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor` additionally require cluster leadership, which is what appends already require.

Leadership is not enough on its own, so the anchor also carries a fencing token. A superseded leader still holds a working handle, and during a handoff two nodes can both believe they hold it — no agreement between processes can settle that, only what is already stored. A purge reads the token before deleting anything and refuses outright if it has been passed, and the anchor write is refused by the database on the same test.

The boundary itself is fenced too, and separately from the token, because a boundary may only ever advance. A leader holding a HIGHER token can still be proposing a smaller range legitimately, and allowing that while another node was midway through deleting a larger one would leave rows above the surviving boundary gone with nothing accounting for them — the one state the anchor exists to make impossible. Held by the database, so no ordering between the two nodes has to be reasoned about.

`b.clusterStorage.fencedUpsert` is that operation, shared with the audit tip, which had the only implementation of it: MySQL can neither express the condition nor report the refusal, so it needs a read-back the other dialects do not, and one copy of that is enough.

items.title: A cluster purge can actually delete the rows it archived
items.body:
`b.frameworkSchema.ensureSchema` installs an append-only BEFORE-DELETE trigger on `audit_log` and `audit_checkpoints` for every dialect — that trigger is why a privileged actor cannot quietly remove an audit row. The cluster branch of the purge deleted straight through it, on the stated assumption that external databases had no such triggers, so a purge against Postgres or MySQL was refused by the guard every time.

With the boundary now recorded before the deletion, that refusal would leave the anchor advanced over rows still present, which verification then skips.

On Postgres the guard is never taken off and never switched off. It decides per row, permitting a DELETE only for a row at or below the boundary the purge anchor records — and the anchor is written before the rows go, so the guard allows exactly what the purge will remove and refuses everything else. Nothing is granted, which matters: a session setting is not an authorization, because `SET LOCAL` is available to any session holding the framework's own role, so a guard that honoured one could be self-granted by exactly the caller it exists to stop. What the guard does not do is worth stating, because the shape invites the opposite assumption: it does not stop a role that can UPDATE the anchor table, which can raise the boundary, delete what widening permits, and restore the signed row before committing. No rule expressible in a trigger closes that, because the same role supplies the input the rule reads. Making it authoritative against the application's own role needs an authorization that role cannot assume — a separate database role owning these tables and granting no UPDATE on the anchor, or append-only storage underneath — which is a deployment decision the schema cannot make for you. The guard covers the rest: an accidental DELETE from application code, and any role holding DML on the audit tables but not on the anchor. The detection that does not depend on privileges is the chain itself, where removing rows above the boundary breaks the hash linkage and removing the newest ones is what the tip sidecar's rollback check catches. **Installing the guard on MySQL needs a privilege worth checking before you upgrade.** With binary logging enabled — the default — MySQL refuses `CREATE TRIGGER` from a role without `SUPER`, and the `TRIGGER` privilege alone is not sufficient (measured on 8.4, where adding `SET_ANY_DEFINER` does not help either). Grant `SUPER` to the role the framework connects as, or set `log_bin_trust_function_creators=1` on the server. Boot now fails with an error naming both, instead of passing MySQL's own message through — a message that mentions neither the audit guard being installed nor the privilege that is missing. It is a failure rather than a warning on purpose: a volume reported as append-only with no guard on it is the worse outcome. MySQL and SQLite carry the same rule, so no dialect drops its guard for a purge any more. MySQL expresses the condition with `IF … THEN SIGNAL …; END IF`; the semicolon inside makes the body compound, which a protocol driver sends as one message — `DELIMITER` is a command-line construct, and the guard had been shaped around a test harness that needed it. SQLite carries the condition in a `WHEN` clause. Both, and Postgres, wrap the comparison in `COALESCE(..., FALSE)`: with no anchor row the comparison is NULL, and a guard that read that as no-restriction would leave the volume that has never authorized a deletion the least protected one.

That closes a window the previous approach left open — while a purge ran, any other connection holding the framework role could delete audit rows too, and a process killed mid-purge left the guard off until the next boot. The guard now stays installed throughout, on every dialect, including `consent_log`'s and every UPDATE guard, which no purge has any reason to touch.

Behind that trigger sat a second defect the deletion had never reached: it built its SQL without the active dialect, so on MySQL the boundary column was double-quoted and read as a string literal — the comparison failed with a truncated-value error rather than deleting anything. Both are fixed, and a cluster purge is now exercised end to end against live Postgres and MySQL rather than through an injected no-op.

items.title: An interrupted purge can be finished by re-running it
items.body:
The boundary is recorded before the rows it covers are deleted, because the two writes cannot be one transaction and the other order fails worse: a fence refused after the deletion would leave rows gone with nothing accounting for them, which no later purge can repair. Recording first means a refusal deletes nothing.

If the deletion then fails, the boundary describes rows that are still present, and verification skips them. Re-running the same archive now completes that deletion instead of being turned away as non-contiguous — read literally it is non-contiguous, and refusing it would have made the only repair available the one thing the guard rejected. Replaying an archive whose range the anchor already names deletes rows that are already gone, so nothing is gained by replaying one either.

"The same archive" means the whole range, not just where it ended. The anchor records `firstPurgedCounter` alongside the boundary and signs it, so an archive that ends at the same counter but starts later is a different, smaller archive and is refused. Without that, such a bundle would have passed as a retry, deleted everything through the boundary, and left the rows before its own start with no retained copy anywhere.

An anchor written before that field was covered still verifies: when the stored range start is `0` — the only value such an anchor can hold, and one that means the same thing in both layouts — verification retries against the shorter signed bytes. Such an anchor is held to the boundary alone when a retry is judged, too: chain counters begin at 1, so a stored `0` records no start rather than claiming one, and requiring it to equal the archive's start would turn away the very bundle that could finish an interrupted purge there — the contiguity check refuses it as well, since the anchor already ends where that archive ends. An anchor claiming a non-zero start gets no second chance, so this cannot be used to drop the field from an anchor that has one, and producing either signature still requires the signing key.

items.title: An audit write stops when the anchor cannot be believed
items.body:
Boot has always refused to start on an audit chain it cannot verify. The same now applies to tampering that happens while the process is running: if the purge anchor is present and does not verify, `b.audit.record` throws `audit/purge-anchor-not-verified` rather than starting a fresh chain.

Starting over looks like the cautious choice and is the opposite. The new rows would link to `ZERO_HASH` and, on a table a purge had emptied, take counters at or below the boundary the anchor claims — the range `verifyChain` skips. Every write between the tampering and the next verification would land there, linked to nothing and invisible to the check meant to catch it. Refusing costs an audit row; the alternative costs the chain its meaning.

items.title: A chain that resumes after a purge keeps its counters
items.body:
`b.audit.record` derived the next `monotonicCounter` from `MAX(monotonicCounter)`, which an emptied table answers with nothing. After a purge that removed every row, the next process restart therefore restarted the counter at 1 — at or below the purge boundary, which is exactly the range `verifyChain` skips. The rows were written, linked correctly to each other, and excluded from every verification that ever ran over them, with nothing reporting it.

The counter now resumes above the recorded boundary, alongside the hash. Both come from the same verified anchor, read once and cached, so neither can be restored without the other. In a cluster that cache also expires when leadership moves: a purge runs on one node, and a node that led before it and leads again after it would otherwise still hold the pre-purge answer and link its next row to nothing — turning a legitimate purge into a reported chain break. The fencing token is what crosses nodes, so an origin read under an earlier term is re-read rather than trusted. The read itself is a database round trip, so the term is checked again once it returns: an origin fetched just before another node purged describes a chain that no longer exists, and noticing on the next append would be too late for the row this one is about to write. Leadership that will not settle refuses the append instead of linking to a boundary that may already be superseded and an append does not pay for a database read per row.

A purge discards that cached answer before it releases the chain lock. A counter primed while the purge was midway through — after the rows were deleted, before the anchor accounting for them was written — would otherwise have survived as 1 for the life of the process.

items.title: A mail TLS pair that will not load says which file is wrong (#672)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.tls.context` refused a bad certificate pair with OpenSSL's own text and named neither file — `error:05800074:x509 certificate routines::key values mismatch` and nothing else. Those are the two commonest operator mistakes with a TLS pair, both arrive at boot with the server refusing to start, and in both cases the next question is which file: a host mid-renewal has several candidates and usually a symlink, and this function is the only thing that knows which pair it just compared.

The refusal now leads with what is wrong in words, lists the certificate and key paths, and keeps the OpenSSL string after them rather than instead of them. Paths only — a key supplied as a vault-sealed blob is named by its path, never by anything it unsealed to.

**An empty or truncated file is now refused at startup instead of accepted.** This came out of testing the above and is the more serious half. `createSecureContext` does not object to a missing certificate — a context without one is what a TLS *client* uses, and is perfectly legal — so a mail server handed an empty `certFile` started cleanly, advertised STARTTLS, and failed every handshake at runtime. An interrupted renewal leaves exactly that file, and the failure surfaced as far as it is possible to get from its cause. A file holding no PEM block is refused by name.

Where the framework knows which file is at fault it names that one; naming both is reserved for the mismatch, where each file is individually fine and only the pair is wrong.

items.title: A failed open no longer leaves the decrypted database behind (#678)
items.body:
Under `atRest: "encrypted"` the live database is a decrypted working copy in `tmpDir`, and `removePlaintextFiles()` is what stops it outliving the process that made it. An open that threw AFTER claiming that copy never reached it: `close()` returned immediately when `initialized` was false, and that flag says only that init did not FINISH — nothing about what it had already taken. So a failed open left plaintext exactly where the design says none persists, in the case nobody is watching, because the caller saw a throw and moved on.

The claim is now tracked in its own right. `close()` releases it, and `b.db.init` releases it itself when it throws, so recovery does not depend on the caller remembering a `close()` in a `catch`. It is deliberately NOT keyed on the working-copy path alone: that path survives a previous open in the same process, and cleaning up on it would delete a different database's copy when an open failed before claiming anything.

Removing the files also closes the database handle first. Windows refuses to unlink a file another handle holds open, and those unlinks swallow their errors — so on a path that never closed the handle, the ownership record beside the copy disappeared while the decrypted database stayed, which in a directory listing reads exactly like a cleanup that worked.

The stale sweep can also see what it leaves. It enumerated names ending in `.db`, and the ownership record is `<name>.db.owner` — so a record whose working copy was gone was invisible to it permanently, one more every time an open failed, in the directory that holds decrypted databases. It now enumerates on the prefix and considers both names as one volume. A record whose owner is still running is left alone, because the claim is written BEFORE the copy exists and that is what a peer mid-open looks like; one whose owner is gone, or that is too damaged to name an owner at all, is reclaimed. That last case is a deliberate departure from the rule governing an actual database, where anything unprovable is left alone: removing a database costs data, while a record accounting for nothing costs only the pile it builds.

A refusal that arrives once the handle is live is the one case where the copy is deliberately kept: if the final re-encryption also fails, removing it would discard migrations and schema work that committed before the verifications ran, while leaving the older encrypted volume in place — so the next boot would re-run migration steps it holds no record of applying. The copy stays, the failed re-encryption is logged, and the ownership record beside it lets a later boot reclaim or adopt it once this process is gone.

items.title: A read-only open no longer tries to migrate the volume it is inspecting
items.body:
`b.db.init({ readOnly: true })` ran the declarative schema reconcile like any other open. That is a no-op only when the live schema already matches the declaration — and a volume written by an earlier version does not match, because it is missing whatever columns that version had not declared yet. Reconcile answered the difference with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, the handle refused the write, and the open failed.

So the flag whose purpose is inspecting a database without touching it worked on every volume except the older ones an inspection is most likely to be about — and this release, which adds two columns to the purge-anchor table, would have made that the common case. A read-only open now takes the schema as it finds it. Every framework read of a possibly-older table already tolerates the columns being absent.

items.title: A DSN is validated in every per-recipient group, and Action is required (#662)
items.body:
`b.mailBounce.dsn.parse` checked `perRecipients[0]` and nothing else. RFC 3464 §2.3 defines the per-recipient group as repeating precisely because a report describes several recipients, and privileges none of them — so a report carrying five groups was validated on one. The other four reached the consumer through `event.raw.allRecipients`, which is the only way to handle a multi-recipient report, carrying an Action token outside §2.3.3 or no recipient at all. Anyone can compose a multipart/report and send it to a postmaster address, so that is unvalidated stranger input returned from a successful parse.

Every group is now held to the same rules, and a bad one refuses the whole report: half a document is not a smaller true statement.

`Action` is also required rather than optional. The previous guard short-circuited on the empty string an absent field produces, so a report stating no verdict parsed cleanly and normalized to `bounce` / `unknown` — indistinguishable downstream from one that claimed something. It is the field that says whether the message failed, was delayed, or was in fact delivered. Reports that genuinely omit it parse under `b.mailBounce.dsn.parse(raw, { requireAction: false })`, which restores the previous normalization.

items.title: A subaddress of the account's own mailbox may be used as a sender (#667)
items.body:
The submission listener's identity binding compared MAIL FROM against the actor's mailbox set by exact match, folding case and nothing else. Where `alice+tag@example.com` is delivered to `alice@example.com` (RFC 5233), the same server routed an address to a mailbox and then refused that mailbox as its sender — one identity, two answers. An MUA configured with a subaddress identity puts it in both `From` and `MAIL FROM`, so the account could not send at all, and the refusal read as the account being wrong rather than the address spelling being unfolded.

Set `subaddressDelimiter` (`"+"` on most systems, `"-"` on qmail-derived ones) and the comparison folds the detail part on both sides. It is off unless set, because subaddressing is a property of the delivery side and this framework does not implement delivery: on a deployment that allocates plus-addresses as distinct mailboxes, folding by default would hand one account send-as authority over another's. The fold reaches only the local part — a different mailbox whose name merely starts with an entry in the set, or the same local part at another domain, is still refused.

For everything a fixed set cannot express — an alias that lands in the account's mailbox, or anything else the consumer resolves at request time — `b.mail.server.submission.create` accepts `senderPolicy(ctx)`, shaped like the MX listener's `recipientPolicy`. It is asked only after the set has declined, so an ordinary send never reaches it, and it fails closed: a policy that throws or rejects refuses the sender rather than admitting one. While one is outstanding the listener holds the client's pipelined commands rather than answering past the MAIL they depend on (RFC 2920).

items.title: An archive's manifest can no longer claim a wider range than the rows it holds
items.body:
`b.auditTools.verifyBundle` checked the first and last row HASHES against the manifest but never the counters, and every other check asks about the rows that are present — so a bundle rewritten to hold rows 51-100 under a manifest still claiming to begin at 1 passed all of them. What that claim then buys is a purge: the boundary is authorized from the claimed start, and rows 1-50 are deleted with no copy of them anywhere.

The manifest's `firstCounter` must now equal the first archived row's counter, and its `lastCounter` must name a row the bundle actually carries. Both are checked in `verifyBundle`, so every caller that reads a bundle inherits them rather than the purge path alone.

items.title: A boot that refuses a database no longer leaves it open
items.body:
The database handle goes live before the chain verifications so that audit and consent can read through the public surface. A verification that refused the boot therefore threw with the handle open, and `b.db.init` never returned — leaving the caller nothing to close it with. The refused database stayed reachable through the public API, and under `atRest: "encrypted"` its decrypted working copy stayed in the temporary directory.

A refusal now closes what that boot opened, re-sealing before removing the plaintext rather than deleting files from under a live handle. It also skips the closing checkpoint a normal shutdown writes: a checkpoint is a signed statement about the state it anchors, and writing one over a state just refused would hand the next boot a fresh anchor for the tampering that stopped this one.

items.title: A purge anchor's archive is bound to its checkpoint as well as its rows
items.body:
The signed anchor covered the digest of the archive's encrypted rows, so a rewritten payload no longer answered for the rows it licensed away. Its covering checkpoint was still checked against the manifest alone — and the manifest travels with the bytes it describes. Replacing `checkpoint.enc` and updating its checksum passed every test `blamejs audit verify-chain --archive-dir` applies, and the command reported the archive producible even though verifying it requires that checkpoint and would fail.

The anchor now signs both digests, and the offline resolver prefers the signed value for each. An anchor written before this field carries an empty one and still verifies, under the payload layout it was signed with.

items.title: A missing anchor table on MySQL reads as an absent anchor, not a failed read
items.body:
Telling "the table is not there yet" from "the query failed" was done by matching the driver's message, and MySQL words it with a contraction — `Table 'db.X' doesn't exist` — that the SQLite and Postgres wordings do not cover. On a MySQL schema without `_blamejs_audit_purge_anchor`, verification stopped with a driver error instead of reading the absence for what it is.

The driver's own structured fields are asked first now, through `b.clusterStorage.missingRelationCode` and `b.clusterStorage.missingColumnCode`, which every caller of that question shares. A failure that says nothing about the schema — a timeout, a permission error — still stops the read: reading it as "there is no anchor" would verify a purged chain from the chain origin and report it clean.

items.title: A rotated-key anchor written under an older payload can be repaired
items.body:
`b.auditChain.verifyPurgeAnchor` recognises an anchor signed before a field joined the payload by retrying the older layouts, each gated on the field it omits still being empty. `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor` rechecked only the current layout, so an anchor that was both written by an earlier build and since re-keyed could not be repaired — and the volume could not boot. Both now ask the same question through `b.auditChain.purgeAnchorSignatureVerifies`.

Reading such an anchor needs the same care. A verifier that opens a database file directly never runs the migration adding those columns, so the read tries the widest projection and narrows when the table lacks one — and it narrows by a single column per step, because a projection that omits a column the table HAS rebuilds the payload with that field's default and reports an untouched anchor as forged. The checkpoint-digest and rows-digest steps were one, so a volume purged between those two builds lost both: its anchor was signed under a layout covering the rows digest, so it rebuilt with an empty one and verification called the volume tampered. The ladder is now derived from the column list rather than written out, so one step per column holds by construction.

items.title: An async hook supplied to the framework can no longer take the process down
items.body:
Every optional callback a consumer hands the framework — `onEvict`, `onProgress`, `onDrop`, `onCorruption`, `onMissingKey`, `onRetry`, `onExit`, the TLS-report `onRefuse` chain, the static-serve `onError` — was called inside a synchronous try/catch and documented as drop-silent. That covered only the hooks that happen not to be async. Writing one as `async function (evt) { await store.record(evt); }` is the ordinary shape, and its rejection arrives a turn after the catch has gone, so it became an unhandled rejection: under Node's default that ends the process, from a callback whose entire contract was that it could not.

All 50 such call sites across 26 modules now route through `b.safeAsync.safeInvoke`, `b.safeAsync.safeApply` or `b.safeAsync.containRejection`, each of which inspects what the callback returned and routes a rejection to the same error path a throw takes. `b.safeAsync.safeInvoke` itself is one of the sites that was affected, so every drop-callback built on it is covered as well.

The worst case was a hook that runs from a socket's close handler, where an escaping rejection has no caller left to catch it: an idle POP3 connection dropping could end a listener process serving every other session on the host.

The same containment now holds for a value that is promise-like without being a promise. A consumer object may return its own thenable — from a session store's `close()`, an audit sink, or any of the hooks above — and the ordinary way to write one is `then(resolve, reject)`, which calls the fulfillment handler it is handed. A real promise ignores a non-callable one, so passing a placeholder looked correct and worked everywhere it was tested; against a hand-written thenable it raised a `TypeError` on a later turn, outside the `try` that was containing failures. Every attachment point now passes a real function, and reads the `then` property inside the guard, since a getter can throw too.

items.title: `blamejs audit verify-chain` resolves its path flags against the working directory it was given
items.body: `--archive-dir` and `--public-key` were passed to the filesystem exactly as typed, while `--db` resolved against the CLI context's working directory. Invoked with a context whose directory differs from the process's, a relative `--archive-dir` searched the wrong place and the command reported the anchored archive missing — a failure indistinguishable from the tampering the check exists to detect.

items.title: Framework DDL quotes its table name, matching every read of it
items.body:
`b.frameworkSchema.setTablePrefix` accepts any valid SQL identifier, and the generated `CREATE TABLE` / `CREATE INDEX` / trigger statements interpolated the resulting name unquoted while `b.sql` quotes identifiers when it builds the queries that read those tables. On Postgres an unquoted identifier folds to lower case, so a mixed-case prefix created `_Blamejs_audit_log` as `_blamejs_audit_log` and the quoted reads then looked for a table that was never there.

Both sides now quote. Under the default all-lowercase prefix the two forms address the identical table on every supported dialect, so nothing changes for a deployment that never set a custom prefix.

items.title: Vendored data and PKI refreshed
items.body:
The bundled public-suffix list is refreshed to its 2026-08-29 revision, and the vendored `@blamejs/pki` to 0.6.5. The suffix list decides cookie-scope and same-site boundaries, so a stale copy misjudges registrable-domain edges for any TLD that changed in between.

The toolkit's own public APIs graduate to stable across those releases, and they add `pki.ocsp.verifyRequest` for responder implementers plus a certificate-level Certificate Transparency verdict (`pki.ct.verifySctList`, `pki.ct.x509CertEntry`, and an optional CT gate on `pki.path.validate`). Later releases in the range add a SCEP enrollment codec (`pki.scep.build` / `pki.scep.parse`, RFC 8894), certs-only certificate-management messages (`pki.cms.certsOnly`, `pki.cms.parseCertsOnly`, `pki.cms.isCertsOnly`, `pki.smime.buildCertsOnly`, RFC 8551), ACME account update and order listing (`updateAccount` and `listOrders` on `pki.acme.client`, RFC 8555), and a CMP key-recovery request body (`krr` on `pki.cmp.build`, RFC 9810). All of it is additive; nothing the framework calls changes behaviour.

items.title: A peer's 5xx refusal is a hard bounce again (#681)
items.body:
`b.mail.send.deliver` classified every delivery attempt from `err.smtpResponse` — a property nothing in the framework ever set. The three response branches of its classifier were therefore unreachable, and every peer refusal fell through to transient: a `550 5.1.1 User unknown` was deferred and retried on the backoff schedule for hours, against every MX host in turn, and the DSN the sender eventually received carried a synthesized timeout reason rather than the receiver's own diagnostic. RFC 5321 §4.2.1 makes the leading digit the whole verdict — a 5yz means the client SHOULD NOT repeat the request — and §4.5.4.1 sets the retry discipline for 4yz only.

The transport now carries the peer's numeric reply on the error it throws, as `statusCode`, and the delivery layer takes its verdict from the transport rather than re-reading the digit — because how far a refusal reaches depends on WHICH command it answered:

- `MAIL FROM`, `DATA`, `BDAT` and the end-of-DATA reply are about this message. A 5yz there is a bounce.
- `RCPT TO` is about one mailbox, so a 5yz is a bounce when the envelope names a single recipient. With several, this transport aborts the transaction on the first refusal, and condemning the message would discard recipients that were never offered.
- A greeting, EHLO or STARTTLS refusal rejects this session with this host. A backup MX may accept the message, so the code travels for diagnostics and the failover continues.
- `AUTH` is the exception among those: a transport that authenticates is talking to one configured relay rather than a set of MX records, so `535` on those credentials is a configuration error no retry resolves.

A failure with no reply at all — a timeout, a socket error, a TLS upgrade that never completed — stays transient, which is what it was. A recipient permanently refused is reported in `failed` with the receiver's code, is not offered to the remaining MX hosts, and reaches `mail.send.deliver.permanent-fail` in the audit feed.

Where a failure has no reply code, its class comes from the error code this framework assigned when it detected the condition, and no longer from words found in the message. A message carries the peer's own reply text, so matching on it let the far side pick its verdict: `451 4.7.0 REQUIRETLS policy service temporarily unavailable` is a request to retry, and the word REQUIRETLS in it counted as the host declining to offer the extension — which for a single-MX domain was the entire evidence set, so the message was bounced `5.7.30` instead of being deferred. The MTA-STS arm ran the same way and is the more dangerous of the two, since its verdict is permanent. An unrecognised failure now falls through to transient, which defers rather than bounces.

items.title: Four PQC signature sizes named the wrong algorithm variant (#682)
items.body:
Comments sizing audit-checkpoint storage quoted SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256**s** figures for the 256**f** default: 29.5 KB where the real signature is 49,856 bytes, so the default signing path was documented at 59% of its size. `b.agentSnapshot` was out by an order of magnitude (~5 KB, which is ML-DSA-87's size), and `b.webhook`'s header-cap budget quoted 40 KB base64url / 59 KB hex where an SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f signature encodes to 66,475 and 99,712 characters.

All four now carry measured byte counts, and a test pins every algorithm's signature size against `node:crypto` so the next drift fails a gate rather than shipping — prose being the one place a wrong number survives every other check.

items.title: REQUIRETLS reaches the wire (#660)
items.body:
`b.mail.send.deliver` carried an operator's `requireTls` flag through the delivery chain into the SMTP transport, which validated ten other options and had no reader for this one. The value arrived and was discarded, so mail left with no REQUIRETLS parameter and a receiver that would have honoured it was never asked. Nothing reported a problem: from the consumer's side the option was accepted, validated and threaded exactly as documented. `b.mail.requireTls.peerSupports` and `b.mail.requireTls.mailFromExtension` — the two functions that decide the question and compose the parameter — had no caller anywhere in the library.

The transport now reads it: `peerSupports` gates it on the post-STARTTLS EHLO response, and the parameter is appended through `mailFromExtension`, beside the SMTPUTF8 and BODY= parameters that were already composed this way. Per RFC 8689 §4.1 a peer that does not advertise the extension is REFUSED rather than delivered to without it — silently downgrading is indistinguishable from success to the consumer that asked.

Whether a peer offers the extension is a property of that host, so the refusal fails over: the next MX gets a turn, which honours the flag rather than violating it. Once every host has been asked and none advertises it, the message is undeliverable (§4.1) and reported as a permanent failure with `5.7.30`, rather than deferred to rediscover the same fact on every retry. A host skipped before the send — a DANE lookup failing mid-rollover — never answered the question, so a run containing one stays deferrable.

`requireTls` is also validated at construction, so a non-boolean is a boot error rather than another silent drop.

items.title: A refused agent handoff chooses its own SMTP reply (#668)
items.body:
Every rejection from `agent.handoff` was answered `451 4.3.0 Local delivery error` on both the submission and MX listeners. A refusal the agent made on policy grounds is permanent, and RFC 5321 §4.2.1 defines 4yz as temporary — so a conforming MTA retried a message that would be refused identically until its own queue lifetime expired. The text named a condition that had not occurred, and whatever the consumer computed reached the audit event and stopped there.

A rejection may now carry `smtpCode` ("550"), `enhancedStatus` ("5.7.1") and `replyText`, and the listener writes them. Each is checked on its own: a code outside 4yz/5yz is not honoured, because a 2yz would tell the peer the message was accepted by the call that refused it; an enhanced status whose class contradicts the code is replaced with that code's class, since a peer reading one would otherwise get the opposite verdict from a peer reading the other; and the text is injection-checked like every other operator string on the wire. A rejection carrying none of them still answers 451 4.3.0, so nothing composed against the old behaviour changes.

items.title: Implicit TLS for the store listeners (#665)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.imap.create`, `b.mail.server.pop3.create` and `b.mail.server.managesieve.create` accept `implicitTls: true`, the mode the submission listener already had for 465. RFC 8314 §3 recommends implicit TLS on 993 and 995 over the in-band upgrade, and it was the one arrangement a consumer could not compose.

The alternative was a TLS terminator in front of 143 / 110 / 4190, and behind one the listener is handed a plaintext connection: it cannot see TLS it is not part of, so every credential is refused, and the greeting advertises STARTTLS inside an established TLS session. A trusted-terminator option would have made an address check the thing standing between a password and the wire, which is what the required `tlsContext` exists to prevent.

The accepted socket is wrapped from the first byte, the session opens with TLS already established, the upgrade verb is neither advertised nor accepted (§3.3), the default port becomes 993 / 995 where the RFC names one, and the listening audit event reports the wire mode. ManageSieve keeps 4190, which is the only port RFC 5804 defines, so there the mode changes how the port speaks rather than which port it is. Off by default.

items.title: A composition point for the IMAP capability line (#664)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.imap.create` accepts `capabilities(caps, state)`, returning the list to advertise. It is applied where the list is COMPUTED, so the three places it is written on one connection — the greeting (RFC 9051 §7.1.5), the answer to `CAPABILITY` (§6.1.1) and the response code completing `AUTHENTICATE` / `LOGIN` — stay identical by construction.

The dispatch registry already accepted a `CAPABILITY` override, but using it produced a server whose three answers disagreed on one connection, so one of them was false whichever way it was set. `IMAP4rev2` is re-added if a hook drops it: §6.1.1 requires it, and a listener that omitted it would be claiming a protocol it does not speak.

items.title: POP3 session-lifecycle hooks (#669)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.pop3.create` accepts `onSessionEnd(actor, sessionId)` and `onSessionActivity(actor, sessionId, verb)`, both optional and absent by default.

RFC 1939 §3 gives a maildrop to one session at a time, so a store leases it exclusively — and had no signal telling it when to let go. A client that loses its link never sends QUIT, so the socket simply goes away and the lease stays held until a timer the consumer guessed at expires. For that window the account holder's own retries are refused, correctly, for a lease genuinely still held. `onSessionEnd` fires exactly once however the session ended: a clean QUIT, an idle timeout, or a link that dropped without either.

`onSessionActivity` fires for every command including NOOP, which is what the protocol offers a client as a keepalive. The listener answers NOOP without touching the store, so a consumer ageing an idle lease on its own accounting never saw the keepalive and reaped the lease under a connection that was still in use.

items.title: `b.safeAsync.safeApply` and `b.safeAsync.containRejection`
items.body:
`b.safeAsync.safeApply(callback, args, onError)` is `b.safeAsync.safeInvoke` for a callback taking more than one argument — a positional list in place of the single payload, identical in every other respect.

`b.safeAsync.containRejection(value, onError)` makes a value safe to ignore: if it is a promise, a rejection reaches `onError` rather than the process, and the value is returned as it came in so a caller that wants to await it still can. It is for the caller that needs the callback's result to decide what happens next — a refusal hook whose response commit determines whether the default refusal still runs.

items.title: A purged chain resumes rather than restarting
items.body:
`b.chainWriter.create` accepts `resolveOrigin`, which the table's owner uses to say where its chain continues when the table holds no rows for a key — `{ hash, counter }`, or nothing, in which case an empty table starts a new chain at `ZERO_HASH` from counter 1 as before. `b.audit` supplies one that reads the verified purge anchor.

`b.audit.withChainLock(fn)` runs `fn` holding the append lock, for a caller that has to change what the chain reads while nothing appends to it.

items.title: `b.time.monotonicMs` and `b.time.stopwatch` (#666)
items.body:
Measuring how long something took had no right answer on `b`. The nearest-looking one, `b.time.monotonicNow`, is not it: its guarantee is ORDERING — values that never repeat and never go backwards — and it is built over `Date.now()`, so an operator correcting the host forward carries that correction into the number, and subtracting two readings reports time that never passed. A consumer was left choosing between the wall clock and hand-rolling `process.hrtime.bigint()`.

`b.time.monotonicMs()` returns milliseconds from a source no clock correction can move. The value means nothing on its own — it counts from an arbitrary point, so it is not a timestamp and cannot be stored or compared across processes — but the difference between two readings is elapsed time. `b.time.stopwatch()` wraps that for the common case, returning a reader with `ms()` and `reset()`. Neither takes a source: a configurable one would let a caller point the steppable-proof primitive back at the wall clock, which is the mistake they exist to prevent.

Use them for anything whose correctness depends on how much time has passed rather than on what time it is — a lease, a rate window, a refill interval, a timeout. A forward correction on a wall-clock-measured lease reaps a lock a session is still holding; on a rate window it hands back the whole budget with no time having passed, so the documented ceiling stops being the ceiling kept.

The framework had four private copies of the conversion, in `metrics`, the request logger, `server-timing` and `stream-throttle`; they now share this one. Two of them carried a `Date.now()` fallback for environments without `hrtime` — unreachable on any supported Node, and the one path that could put a correctable clock behind a duration, including a negative one on a host stepped backwards mid-request. Those are gone with the local conversions.

`b.time.monotonicNow`'s documentation now says what it is not for, since its name is what a reader looking for elapsed time finds first.

items.title: The boot clock check can be authenticated (BLAMEJS_NTS_SERVERS)
items.body:
The framework ships an RFC 8915 NTS client, and the shipped compose files declared `BLAMEJS_NTS_SERVERS` and `BLAMEJS_NTS_REQUIRE` — which nothing read. An operator who set them got the plain SNTP check they were trying to replace, and no signal that the setting had done nothing.

That matters because this reading decides whether the process refuses to boot. An unauthenticated SNTP reply is whatever the network says it is, so someone on the path can force a refusal, or hold a drifting clock inside the thresholds, and the check cannot tell.

`b.ntpCheck.checkDrift` and `b.ntpCheck.bootCheck` now take `ntsServers` and try them first, reporting `authenticated: true` when the answer came from one and `false` when it came from plain SNTP — stated explicitly, so a caller cannot read a missing field as a guarantee. `BLAMEJS_NTS_SERVERS` supplies that list at boot.

Falling back to unauthenticated time remains the default, because most hosts have no NTS server configured and refusing them would be a boot failure nobody asked for. `BLAMEJS_NTS_REQUIRE=1` refuses the boot unless an authenticated reading was obtained — including when the check could not be completed at all, since a check that did not finish has not met the requirement. That covers a time server that never answered, a server list that could not be parsed, a checker that would not load, and `BLAMEJS_SKIP_NTP_CHECK=1`: where two settings contradict each other, the one asking for a guarantee wins, and the refusal names the setting that turned the check off.

Each entry is `host`, `host:port`, or `[ipv6]:port`, and an entry that cannot be parsed — a port outside 1-65535, a non-numeric port, an unclosed bracket, an empty host — is refused at boot rather than treated as a server that failed to answer. A malformed port used to fall back to the NTS-KE default, which meant contacting a different endpoint than the one configured.

`b.ntpCheck.checkDrift` validates its opts against a schema, so a field present with the wrong type is refused instead of read as absent. Three of those were silent: a string `requireNts` (`"true"` from a config loader) read as DISABLED and fell back to unauthenticated time; a non-array `ntsServers` read as an empty list and attempted no authenticated query; and a string `servers` has a length and indexes, so it was walked character by character — `servers: "zq"` queried the hosts `z` and `q`, never contacted the configured server, and reported an ordinary unreachable warning while the clock went unchecked. A key the schema does not declare is refused as well, so a typo in an option name cannot be silently ignored. `db.init` builds a real boolean and a real array from the environment and was never affected; this reached callers using the API directly.

`b.ntpCheck.bootCheck` and `b.ntpCheck.monitor` validate the same way, so the three agree about options they share. `bootCheck` read its `driftWarnMs` / `driftFatalMs` overrides with a `typeof` test and fell back to the registered thresholds when they were not numbers, so a string override was dropped and the boot ran against a value the caller had not asked for. Zero stays valid on both: it disables that threshold. `monitor` validates before it starts its timer rather than inside the tick, which caught its own error and returned — a mistyped option previously produced a live-looking monitor handle whose every clock check failed silently.

The numeric clock settings are checked where they are read, so a typo cannot change clock policy in silence. `BLAMEJS_NTP_TIMEOUT_MS`, `BLAMEJS_NTP_DRIFT_WARN_MS` and `BLAMEJS_NTP_DRIFT_FATAL_MS` must each be a whole number of milliseconds; a value that is not one refuses the boot and names the variable, where before it parsed to `NaN` and was absorbed — the timeout skipped the clock check entirely, and a bad threshold was swallowed at debug level while the registered default quietly stayed in force. A warn threshold above the fatal one is refused for the same reason: it is a policy that cannot be satisfied. Zero remains valid on both thresholds and disables that one.

items.title: An unreachable time server can now be made to refuse the boot (#684)
items.body:
When no NTP server answered, `b.ntpCheck.bootCheck` returned a warning whose message told the operator to `set BLAMEJS_NTP_STRICT=1 to fail closed`. Following that changed nothing: the variable already defaults to `1`, and the only code that reads it is the branch handling excessive drift, which an unreachable server never reaches. There was no setting that made an unanswered query fail closed, so a host with outbound UDP/123 blocked booted on an unchecked clock indefinitely while being told it had a way to prevent that.

`BLAMEJS_NTP_REQUIRE_REACHABLE=1` is that way, and the message now names it. It is opt-in rather than default-on because a network without outbound NTP is ordinary and refusing every such host would be a boot failure nobody asked for; only a query that went unanswered qualifies, since a drift reading inside the thresholds is also a warning and the clock was checked there.

The surrounding documentation was wrong in the other direction too, and is corrected: drift past the fatal threshold refuses the boot by DEFAULT, and `BLAMEJS_NTP_STRICT=0` is what downgrades that refusal to a log line.

items.title: `middleware.rateLimit` and `mail.server.rateLimit` accept a clock (#685)
items.body:
Both measured their windows with the wall clock and accepted no `clock` option, while 27 other primitives take one — including `b.auth.lockout` and `b.cache`, the two an application pairs with a rate limiter to build a single coherent failure budget. So an application could put every budget it owned on a monotonic reading and still have two it could not reach.

The windows are comparisons against stored timestamps rather than counters that decay, so a clock step forward — an NTP correction, a virtual machine resuming from a snapshot, an operator fixing a wrong clock — retired every recorded failure at once: an address at the per-IP authentication-failure cap was admitted again immediately, and a sign-in window that was partway through was simply over.

The seam has to be inside the primitive, because the timestamps are taken at write time and compared at read time with no point in between for a caller to substitute its own reading. `middleware.rateLimit` enumerates its accepted option names and refuses the rest, so a caller passing the same clock it gave `auth.lockout` was rejected rather than ignored. Both now take `clock` and thread it through every window they own — the token-bucket refill, the fixed-window rollover, and every rolling window in the mail listener's limiter.

Not the cluster backend, which refuses it. That window is shared: its boundary is `floor(now / windowMs) * windowMs`, written into a row every node upserts against, keeping whichever boundary is newer. Nodes reading different clocks would stop sharing a window, the node running ahead would keep resetting the shared counter, and the cluster-wide limit would not be the limit anyone got. A process-local monotonic reading is precisely what a caller supplies here and nothing can distinguish it from an epoch-accurate one, so the combination is refused at configuration rather than quietly ignored.

A mistyped `clock` is refused at configuration too, along with `keyFn` and `onDeny`. `middleware.rateLimit` catches a throwing backend and fails open, so a clock that was a number rather than a function would not have raised an error — it would have stopped limiting every request while the process reported itself healthy.

items.title: UID SEARCH and LOGIN receive their literal payloads (#686)
items.body:
A client sends any argument that a quoted string cannot carry — a non-ASCII search term, a password with special characters, a UTF-8 mailbox name — as a literal. `b.mail.server.imap` dispatches handlers with the literal as a fourth argument, so a handler declaring three parameters discarded it by arity.

`UID SEARCH` dropped it twice over: once at the `UID` entry, and again where `UID` dispatches its sub-command without forwarding one, so repairing either alone left the command failing `BAD`. The same term over plain `SEARCH` worked, through the same handler, and RFC 9051 sec. 6.4.9 defines the two as taking identical arguments.

The drop was a property of arity rather than of `UID`, so the neighbours were checked rather than assumed. `LOGIN` had it: a password sent as a literal never reached authentication, and the login failed as though the credential were wrong. `SELECT` and `EXAMINE` had it for mailbox names. All are fixed, and a literal is taken verbatim rather than re-quoted — a client sends one precisely when the value cannot be expressed as a quoted string. `APPEND` and `SETMETADATA` already declared the parameter and were unaffected.

items.title: A purge anchor binds the manifest that opens its archive
items.body:
The signed anchor already covered the digests of the archive's encrypted payloads, so a rewritten `rows.enc` or `checkpoint.enc` was caught. It did not cover the manifest — and the manifest carries the salts the decryption key is derived from.

So an attacker able to edit the archive directory could change `salts.rows` alone. Both payloads stay byte-identical, both signed digests still match, every check a reader performs still passes, and `blamejs audit verify-chain --archive-dir` reports the archive producible — while the key derived from that salt opens nothing. The anchor is the one statement that licenses rows to be missing, and it was licensing them against an archive that could not be read.

The anchor now carries `archiveManifestDigest`, signed with the rest, and the resolver checks the bundle's manifest against it. The digest covers the canonical manifest rather than the file's raw bytes, so reformatting is not a refusal while any change to a value it carries is.

An anchor written before this field existed verifies through the `no-manifest-digest` layout, exactly as the earlier fields are handled: the retry is offered only while the column is empty, so a volume purged by an earlier build still verifies and an anchor that records a digest gets no retry that omits one.

items.title: The in-memory tmpDir check asks the kernel what is mounted (#690)
items.body:
Under `atRest: "encrypted"` the live database is a decrypted working copy, and `tmpDir` is where it lives. Whether that path was in memory was decided by comparing its NAME against `/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/run/user/` and `/tmp` — a comparison that cannot see what filesystem is mounted anywhere, and that was wrong in two directions.

Three of the four comparisons had no trailing separator, so any path merely BEGINNING with one of those strings passed: `/tmpdata`, `/dev/shmx`, `/run/shm-backup`. The one that mattered more is quieter: a host where `/tmp` is ordinary disk is entirely normal, and there the check said nothing at all — not a refusal, not the `allowNonTmpfsTmpDir` warning — while the whole plaintext database was written where backup snapshots, replication and forensic disk images reach it. That is the threat encryption at rest exists to address, and the operator was told the residency was fine.

The mount table is read instead, through `b.safeMountInfo`, and only `tmpfs` or `ramfs` is accepted. A directory somebody created by hand is not a mount point, so it resolves to whatever filesystem contains it, which is the right answer for it. A mount table that cannot be read reports the residency as UNKNOWN — a warning — rather than as a pass, because the check exists to distinguish those two cases. Hosts running on a disk-backed `tmpDir` will now be told so at boot; `allowNonTmpfsTmpDir: true` accepts the tradeoff explicitly, and `atRest: 'plain'` is the answer where encryption at rest is not required.

items.title: IMAP and ManageSieve enforce the literal byte-rate floor they document (#689)
items.body:
Both listeners document a minimum body rate, build the limiter that enforces one, and never asked it. The only bound on a literal transfer was the idle timeout, which every arriving byte resets — so a peer trickling one byte at a time held a connection slot for as long as it liked. The floor was validated at construction, defaulted, and exposed as a getter no listener called; `b.mail.server.mx` and `b.mail.server.submission` were given it and these two were left out.

IMAP's exposure did not require an account. The literal window was opened from the parsed command shape alone, while the authentication check is the first line of each handler — and handlers run only after the whole literal has been buffered. An unauthenticated peer could therefore open a window on `APPEND`, which the protocol's own state table lists as available only after login, and hold the connection indefinitely without ever presenting a password. The authorization now happens before the resource is committed, with `LOGIN` and `AUTHENTICATE` allowed to carry a literal beforehand because a password is exactly the value a quoted string cannot always hold.

Both listeners now measure the rate at the wire funnel, over bounded windows so an early burst cannot buy credit for a slow tail, and close a connection whose literal falls below the floor. On ManageSieve that covers the `AUTHENTICATE` initial response as well as `PUTSCRIPT` — the authentication literal is the one a peer can open before proving anything, and each transfer gets its own measurement window rather than inheriting the previous one's start time.

items.title: A device binding that reports itself stored is stored (#687)
items.body:
`b.sessionDeviceBinding.create({ storeInSession: true })` never persisted anything. The write went through `b.session.touch`, which reads `opts.extendBy` and nothing else — both of its SQL paths carry a static SET list, so the metadata was accepted and discarded. It still returned true, because it had updated `lastActivity` on a live session, so nothing threw and the audit row recorded `stored: true` for a binding that was never written. Every later `verify()` answered `missing-bind`, which a consumer enforcing on it reads as a reason to refuse every session it has bound.

The fingerprint is now written through `b.session.updateData` — the session's sealed data payload, which is where `verify()` was already looking for it — merged so it does not displace whatever else the application keeps there, and the stored flag comes from that call's return value rather than from the absence of an exception. `create()` requires a session exposing `updateData` rather than `touch`: it was checking for the one capability every session object has and the feature could not use.

The binding lives under a key the payload path cannot write. `b.session.create`, `updateData` and `rotate` all ignore `__bj_deviceBinding` supplied in caller data and carry the stored value forward instead, the way `__bj_fingerprint` has always been treated — otherwise an ordinary payload write could clear a binding, or install one, and strict verification would agree. If your application happened to use a key of that name, its value is no longer stored.

A session-backed binding also expires on the same `ttlMs` an external `bindingStore` is given; it previously accepted the option and never applied it. With both stores configured the external one leads and the session is a fallback: a failed external write is kept in the session so the fresh session is not lost, `verify` reads the session when the external store reports no entry, and a later successful external write clears the older session copy. An external store that cannot be READ still refuses (`store-error`) rather than falling back, so an unreachable store cannot quietly downgrade to whatever the session carries.

`create()` also checks the types of `clock` and `storeInSession`, which it previously accepted and used unchecked. Both failed in the direction that hides: `boundAt: clock()` runs inside bind's drop-silent catch, so a non-function `clock` made `bind()` write nothing while reporting `stored: false`, and every later `verify()` answered `missing-bind`; and `storeInSession` was coerced with `!!`, so the string `"false"` switched ON the session-backed store an operator had just switched off.

items.title: A queue retries for as long as RFC 5321 asks (#692)
items.body:
`b.mail.send.deliver` gave up after 81 minutes. RFC 5321 §4.5.4.1 puts the give-up time at 4-5 days, and the difference is mail that would have been delivered once a receiver came back from a maintenance window.

Two causes. `retry.maxAttempts` defaulted to the backoff ramp's LENGTH, and N attempts are separated by N-1 waits — so the ramp's last and longest rung was never reached and the schedule the ramp described was not the one the queue ran. The default ramp also stopped at four hours. The attempt count is now derived as one more than the number of waits, and the ramp runs 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 4h, 8h, 12h, then daily, giving up after just over four days.

The attempt count is also derived from the ramp the CALLER supplied rather than from the default constant's length, which is what made a two-rung ramp still run five attempts and repeat its last wait. `deliver.retryPolicy()` reports the resolved `maxAttempts`, `backoffMs` and `giveUpMs`, so when a queue gives up is readable rather than derived from two options and an off-by-one.

items.title: An expunge refuses a message whose arrival time it cannot establish (#691)
items.body:
`b.mail.agent.expunge` enforces a retention floor under a compliance posture, and read an absent arrival time as 0 — the epoch. A message with no recorded timestamp therefore looked decades old and cleared every floor there is, so the one input the check could not verify was the one that always passed it, and the failure fell toward permitting destruction on exactly the volumes a floor is configured to protect.

An arrival time that cannot be established now refuses the deletion with `retention-floor-unknown-arrival`. The value is checked with `b.numericBounds.isNonNegativeSafeInt`, which also refuses the range above 2^53 where a BIGINT read out of a backend collapses onto a shared Number and two different timestamps stop being distinguishable.

items.title: `middleware.attachUser` forwards the fingerprint basis (#688)
items.body:
`attachUser` enumerates the option names it accepts and refuses the rest, and `fingerprintFields` was not among them — so the only session-binding policy reachable through the middleware was the default basis, which includes the full client address. An operator who deliberately bound sessions on a narrower basis at `session.create` had strict enforcement applied against a basis they had opted out of, and a client that changes address mid-session was signed out for it.

`fingerprintFields` now forwards to `b.session.verify`, along with `trustedProxies` and `clientIpResolver` — resolving the client address is what the default basis depends on, and getting it wrong is what makes the binding wrong. Each is passed only when supplied, so `verify`'s own defaults still apply when they are not.

items.title: A listener at its connection ceiling says so (#693)
items.body:
`maxConnections` closes a connection beyond the ceiling before the handler ever runs, which is what makes it cheap — and meant it produced no audit row, no protocol line and no log. A listener at capacity, turning real senders away, was indistinguishable from an idle one, and the first evidence an operator got was somebody reporting they could not connect.

The refusal is now emitted as `<listener>.max_connections_refused` with the peer address and the ceiling it hit, recorded as a denial. It is emitted from the socket-drop signal, because by design nothing downstream of that point runs.

items.title: A POP3 cleartext refusal checks the auth budget before spending it (#683)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.pop3` refuses a credential verb over a plaintext connection and counts that refusal against the per-IP auth-failure budget, so a scanner probing for plaintext tolerance spends budget doing it. Four of those branches — `USER`, `PASS`, `APOP` and `AUTH` — counted the refusal before asking whether the address was still admitted, and `USER` had no admittance check on its path at all.

The budget is a rolling window over recorded failure times, not a counter that decays: admittance prunes entries older than the window and refuses once enough remain. An address already at the cap that keeps adding entries therefore holds its own window populated and pushes the end of its wait forward, and the refusals cost it nothing — no credential is verified and the connection is not closed. A client looping a plaintext `USER` could hold its own address, and every client sharing it, out of the listener indefinitely without ever presenting a password. It is reachable on a plaintext listener under the balanced profile.

All four now consult the cap first and close the connection when it is spent, matching every other listener. The check is one helper rather than a block per branch, which also settles a smaller drift: of the three that existed, only the one on `PASS` emitted `mail.server.pop3.auth_rate_limit_refused`, so two thirds of these refusals were invisible to an operator watching that event.

items.title: `sec-17a-4` and `finra-4511` are settable compliance postures
items.body:
`b.db` refuses to boot under a records-preservation posture unless row-level WORM has been declared, and it names three: SEC Rule 17a-4(f), FINRA Rule 4511, and FDA 21 CFR Part 11. Only the third was in the posture catalog, so `b.compliance.set("sec-17a-4")` and `b.compliance.set("finra-4511")` were refused as unknown — which meant `b.compliance.current()` could never return them and the boot refusal was unreachable for two of the three regimes it cites. `b.db.declareWorm` accepts any posture string, so the documented example declaring WORM under `sec-17a-4` worked while the posture it referred to could not be entered.

Both are now in the catalog with their citations, so an operator running under either gets the boot-time check the regime requires. `b.compliance.describe` resolves them like any other posture.

items.title: `b.clusterStorage.duplicateIndexCode`
items.body:
The third driver-error predicate, beside `b.clusterStorage.missingRelationCode` and `b.clusterStorage.missingColumnCode`. MySQL has no `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`, so an idempotent schema pass re-issues the plain statement and has to tell "the index is already there" from a statement that genuinely failed.

That was decided by testing the error message for `exist`, which is a substring of both answers MySQL can give: `Duplicate key name 'X'` and `Table 'db.X' doesn't exist`. A `CREATE INDEX` that failed because its table was absent matched the swallow condition too, so the error was discarded and the pass reported the schema reconciled with the index never created. The predicate reads the driver's own `errno` 1061 / `ER_DUP_KEYNAME` instead, which states it exactly and in any locale. It deliberately does not accept SQLSTATE 42000 on its own, because MySQL uses that as the catch-all for syntax and access errors, and accepting it would swallow a malformed statement as an already-present index.

Both schema reconcilers compose it.

items.title: `b.clusterStorage.fencedUpsert`
items.body:
Upsert a single row only if the caller's fencing token is at least the one already stored, and report whether it was refused. This is how a single-writer table stays single-writer across processes, and it is one primitive rather than a shape each caller re-derives because the three dialects disagree about it: Postgres and SQLite take a `WHERE` on the conflict clause and report the refusal by returning no rows, while MySQL's `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` has neither and its fence becomes a per-column `IF()` that changes nothing while still succeeding. Detection there has to read the token back afterwards.

`fenceColumns` names several columns that must ALL be non-decreasing, for a value that may only ever advance — a boundary, a high-water mark. Holding that in the database rather than in whoever writes next is the difference between an invariant and a convention, and a writer with the right token can still be proposing the wrong direction.

items.title: `b.auditSign.pinnedKeyResolver`, `b.auditSign.canonicalPublicKeyPem` and `b.auditSign.publicKeyLicensingDeletion`
items.body:
Three small primitives for naming a key, extracted because the same rule was being restated at each place a key is supplied and drifting between them.

`canonicalPublicKeyPem(pem)` re-exports a key through the parsed form, giving one spelling for one key. `pinnedKeyResolver(pem)` builds a `resolvePublicKey` for a single operator-supplied key that answers for either fingerprint that key can legitimately carry — the text as supplied and the re-export — and nothing else; `blamejs audit verify-chain --public-key` and `db.init({ purgeAnchorPublicKey })` both route through it, so a key saved with different line endings resolves the same either way. `publicKeyLicensingDeletion(fingerprint)` answers for the live signing key alone, which is what a purge anchor is verified against.

items.title: `b.auditChain.verifyPurgeAnchor` and `b.auditChain.purgeAnchorPayload`
items.body: The verification a caller needs when reading an audit database it did not open through `b.db.init` — a forensic check, a restore validation, a downstream auditor. `verifyPurgeAnchor(row, { resolvePublicKey })` takes the key from the caller when the process has none of its own; `purgeAnchorPayload(anchor)` builds the canonical signed bytes.

items.title: `blamejs audit verify-chain --public-key` and `--archive-dir`
items.body:
The command opens a database file directly and never initializes signing, so it holds no key with which to check the anchor that licenses any deleted rows. Point `--public-key` at the audit-signing public key and the anchor is verified; without it, a purged chain now exits 3 (`UNCHECKED`) rather than claiming a verification it did not perform. The key is parsed and re-exported before its fingerprint is taken, so the same key saved with different line endings is still the same key. `audit-sign.pubkeys.json` records keys rotated out, so an anchor signed before a rotation can still be resolved from the PEM it holds. That file is unsealed, which is what lets a verifier read it with no passphrase — so an entry now has to hash to the fingerprint it is filed under. Without that check, anyone able to write the file could file their own key under an expected fingerprint, sign a boundary with the matching private key, and have verification accept it, never touching the wrapped key. Both lookups over that file run the same check. Making an entry hash to its own label stops one key being filed under another's name, but it cannot make an unsealed file AUTHORITATIVE — generating a keypair and adding a self-consistent entry for it needs no secret — so a rotated-out key no longer licenses deleted rows at all. Only the live key does, and it lives sealed behind a passphrase the process had to be given. A checkpoint signed before a rotation still verifies from the history, because attesting that a tip existed only adds a claim; a purge anchor erases, which is a different weight. **Rotating the audit-signing key on a volume that has purged now needs one more step:** call `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor()` afterwards to re-sign the anchor under the new key. Until then the chain refuses to verify and says so, naming that call. Rotating and re-signing are two calls, so a process can exit between them and leave a volume whose anchor names the outgoing key — and the repair needs a booted database, which is what the refused anchor prevents. `db.init({ acceptRotatedPurgeAnchorKey: true })` is the way back in: one boot, it re-signs under the live key and then does nothing. It stays a flag rather than an automatic fixup because the evidence that the anchor verifies under the old key comes from the unsealed history, and re-signing on that alone would launder a planted key into the live one. The flag is the operator saying they performed the rotation. The same reasoning removed a fallback under `auditSigning: false`: with no key loaded, boot used to resolve the anchor's key from that unsealed history, which is the attacker vouching for themselves one configuration over. It no longer does — the anchor reports as unchecked, which that posture already permits, so the volume opens and nothing claims a proof it did not make. An operator who wants it genuinely verified there passes `db.init({ purgeAnchorPublicKey })`, a trust root they chose, still bound to the fingerprint the anchor names. It reports the anchor as naming a rotated-out key rather than as a forgery, because it is not one, and the re-sign checks the existing signature under that rotated key first so a tampered anchor cannot be laundered into a valid one, and `b.auditChain.verifyChain` repeats it at the point of use: the key a purge anchor is verified under must hash to the fingerprint the anchor names. `resolvePublicKey` is an extension point, so without that the binding would hold only as far as each resolver was careful, and one returning a key the anchor does not name yields a signature that verifies perfectly against the wrong key. A key is also matched on the text it was stored as WELL as on a re-export: `rotateSigningKey` records an operator-supplied key exactly as written, so one saved with CRLF line endings was fingerprinted that way, and hashing only a re-export would report those volumes as signed by an unknown key. Supplied keys are canonicalized when they are ingested now, so one key has one spelling from here on.

`--archive-dir` says where archive bundles live. With it, an anchor naming an archive that is not there fails the verify; without it, the result names the archive and states plainly that nothing resolved it. Bundles are matched by the identifier inside their own manifest, together with the range the anchor signed, rather than by directory name, which the operator chooses, and a bundle whose encrypted rows are missing does not count as found, nor does one missing the covering checkpoint an archive cannot be read back without, nor one whose payload no longer hashes to the digest **the anchor signed for it**. That digest is the load-bearing part: a manifest states its own checksums and travels with the bytes it describes, so an attacker who replaces `rows.enc` replaces the checksum beside it and the two still agree — comparing them shows only that the bundle is consistent with itself. The anchor records the digest of the archive the purge actually verified, inside the signed payload, so which bytes the archive has to be is a claim only the signing key can make. A replacement that is internally perfect is refused — present is not the same as intact, and a blob altered in place decrypts to nothing. The range matters because the identifier is the covering checkpoint's, and one checkpoint can cover several archived slices: on the identifier alone, a surviving sibling would answer for the slice that went missing — a manifest naming the right archive is not the archive.

The result also says which range that archive covers. Each purge replaces the anchor, so after several contiguous ones the boundary licenses everything below it while the row names only the newest bundle; letting one resolved archive stand for the whole licensed range would claim a recoverability nothing checked.

items.title: Additive column migration for framework tables
items.body:
`b.frameworkSchema.ensureSchema` issues `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` for columns declared on a table that already exists. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` is a no-op against a table that is already there, so before this a column added to a framework table reached only fresh deployments and the first write naming it failed everywhere else.

The ALTER is generated from the same column declaration the CREATE is built from, so the two cannot disagree, and a column that is NOT NULL without a DEFAULT is refused at build time rather than failing against live data — no engine can fill one for rows that already exist.

items.title: `b.frameworkSchema.withDeleteTriggersSuspended`
items.body:
Runs a function with the append-only BEFORE-DELETE triggers dropped from the cluster audit tables, then puts them back — including the anchor boundary they carry, so what is restored is the same guard and not an unconditional one wearing its name.

Nothing in the framework takes this route. Every dialect's guard is bounded by the purge anchor and stays installed through a purge, so this exists for an operator performing a supervised removal by hand; it grants nothing they could not do with `DROP TRIGGER` themselves.

Understand the cost before calling it. A `DROP TRIGGER` is global: for as long as the function runs, any connection holding the framework role can delete audit rows. The triggers are restored in a `finally` so they come back whether the body succeeded or threw, a table that could not be restored is named in the error, and a process killed mid-call leaves them off until the next `ensureSchema`, which every boot runs.

`dialect` is required and accepts `mysql` or `sqlite`. Postgres is not supported: its guard is a trigger FUNCTION shared by every WORM table, so dropping the triggers and restoring them is not the same operation there.

items.title: An installation that has already purged needs one boot with `acceptUnsignedPurgeAnchor: true`
items.body:
A purge performed by 0.18.57 or earlier left an anchor with no signature, which this release refuses. Re-running the purge does not produce a signed one: the contiguity guard requires an archive starting one counter past the recorded boundary, and the boundary is what is in question.

So boot once with `b.db.init({ acceptUnsignedPurgeAnchor: true })`. That signs the anchor in place, pinning the boundary it already claims so it can never be moved again, and logs what it pinned. Then remove the flag — it does nothing afterwards, and a second run reports that the anchor is already signed rather than rewriting it.

This pins the boundary rather than proving it. Nothing can distinguish a boundary an earlier version wrote from one somebody else did, which is why the signature exists; an operator who needs the boundary proven verifies the retained archive against the chain with `b.auditTools.verifyBundle` before running it. `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor()` is the operation itself, callable directly. It refuses a corrupt or already-forged anchor rather than pinning it — that would turn a detectable problem into a permanent one.

A deployment running `b.db.init({ auditSigning: false })` is unaffected. It has no key to sign with, so it writes unsigned anchors and accepts them; the writer allows exactly what the verifier allows.

Deployments that have never purged have no anchor and need nothing.
